Affiliation:: School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Oklahoma
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Data-Driven Modeling from Measurements: Using observed time-series data to discover the governing equations of a complex system. (e.g., Applying the SINDy algorithm to voltage waveform data from an IEEE 15-bus power grid simulation to identify the mathematical models of its dynamics under different conditions).

Quantifying and Distinguishing Nonlinearity: Developing and applying novel metrics and algorithms to precisely measure and categorize different types of nonlinear behavior. (e.g., Using the SINDy algorithm to separate dynamics into first-order (linearizable) and second-order (nonlinear) terms, and introducing the Volterra-based Nonlinearity Index (VNI) to quantify the nonlinear-to-linear relationship).

System-Level Perspective over Component-Level Solutions: Analyzing problems as emergent properties of the entire network's configuration rather than as localized component failures. (e.g., Investigating how the topological configuration and relative electrical distance of coupled inverters—a system-level property—can create a "harmonic cancellation effect," rather than just focusing on component-level filters).

Socio-Technical Systems Integration: Modeling the interdependent relationship between human behavior (social) and physical infrastructure (technical) as a single system. (e.g., Conceptualizing a two-layer model where an "information layer" (disinformation on social media) influences "user behavior," which in turn causes disruptions in a "physical layer" (critical networks like power grids or transportation)).
Summary Description: Dr. John N. Jiang specializes in Power Systems and Critical Network Risk, exploring their interplay with Nonlinear Dynamics, Machine Learning, and Disinformation. His research examines complex system behaviors, including system-level nonlinearity, the impact of Inverter-Based Resources (IBRs), interaction harmonics, and the risk of disinformation weaponized against infrastructure. He applies data-driven techniques like Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) and Hankel Alternative View of Koopman (HAVOK) to identify models from measurement data. Significant contributions include developing novel mixed algorithms (SINDy+HAVOK), quantifying nonlinearity (e.g., Volterra-based Nonlinearity Index), and modeling the socio-technical link between information and physical grid disruptions.
